chapter: Buck and Bubbles: Nazarro and Bubbles
title: Why Bubbles' cramp roll was richer and progressive
summary: The interviewers and Green compare the kick cramp to the walking cramp, noting more beats and use of the whole body, and that Bubbles invented it.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Watching you do those cramps, Chuck, the John Bubbles and then the Bill Bailey, I must say I felt that John Bubbles' cramp was much richer. It seemed fuller. Of course, you were using both feet. So that that would be the reason why. More than like the Bill Bailey cramp, was just on one foot. Of course, they both look very progressive, extremely progressive, to me. Very sharp. Do you want to tell us about that?
Yeah, well, they were.
I mean, I can understand you being -- admiring John Bubbles so much, by seeing that fabulous kick cramp.
Well, that was the one that was always
magical to the other tap dancers. And he was always trying to get them to relate themselves to these cramps.
Of course there are that many more beats in the John Bubbles cramp.

Much more, because he used the whole body. He used -- like he would jump. He would jump and hop, see, and by -- as he'd come down, as he'd land from the jump, he'd kick with the other foot, and the hop would come after the kick with the other foot, see. So --
It's visually and musically much fuller.
Yes.

Of course, because with the Bill Bailey cramp, it's just the one foot, which is also as progressive, too, from a person just walking. You would walk with that one foot cramp. You could do it like on each foot and use that to get around a stage and make a nice rhythm.
Yeah.

Whereas the one with Bojangles, it looked to me like you're getting into tricks there as well. You know, it's like practically a tour de force, you start doing those things. It's extremely progressive. What would you say about that?
Well, as I say, I used the same system of diplomacy on Mr. Bill Bailey as I did on Mr. Bubbles, you

see. I would teach myself. If I learned a new step, I'd teach myself a way to do the step more than one way, so I learned myself how to do Mr. Bailey's walk cramp, you know, a different way, which as I say, I finally got up to the "A Frain," the melody of Duke Ellington, you see.
In other words, you were being inspired -- all the great steps. You were looking for all the progressive steps.
That's it.
Which is why you dance so great, of course.
I like to stay in the augments. I like to base my dancing,my tap dancing, on the jazz in the augments.
You didn't stand still.
No.
Always progressing.
Yes.
Which is why it sounds so --

Yes. See, because Mr. Bubbles, when he performed anywhere, like if he would be a celebrity somewhere, someone would introduce him from an audience, and Mr. Buck wasn't there, why Mr. Bubbles would get up and he would teach himself how to do a single, you see. Because he was actually a single at that time, but they were so popular as a team, that still and all he'd have to represent Buck and Bubbles. So
naturally he'd have to be perhaps twice as good on his own as he would be with Buck and Bubbles, you see.
And of course the cramp roll is a progressive step in itself, because it's made up of that many more beats. John Bubbles developed the cramp.
Yes, he did. He invented that. He invented that style of tap dancing.
